hallmark: the unbroken oval of pronotum and wing cases, and the hairy pygidium left uncovered behind them

reference.title: Melolontha viridi-aenea, from An epitome of the natural history of the insects of New Holland, plate 1

doc: *Anoplognathus viridiaeneus*, dorsal - the king Christmas beetle.
Traced from plate 1 of Edward Donovan's *An epitome of the natural history
of the insects of New Holland* (1805), where the animal is figured and named
*Melolontha viridi-aenea* - the description Donovan published it under, and
the reason his plate is the type figure for the species.
`references/anoplognathus-viridiaeneus.jpg` is that figure, cut from the
sheet and turned upright; the whole plate carries nine beetles and this is
the large one in the middle.
## What identifies it
Size and shape, before colour. It is one of the largest Christmas beetles -
28 to 34 mm - and the outline is one unbroken oval from the front of the
clypeus to the apex of the wing cases, because the pronotum is at its widest
exactly where the elytra begin. Then the **pygidium**, uncovered behind the
wing cases, and the broad squared **clypeus** at the front. All three are
drawn.
The colour is not drawn and cannot be: red-brown under a gold-green sheen
that shifts with the angle it is held at. `morphology.colourFamily` says
`metallic`, which is where that fact belongs - the same call the rose chafer
made.
## The figure leans, and the plate does not
Donovan's beetle is rolled onto its left side by something like twenty
degrees, and cocks its head a few more. A roll about the long axis
foreshortens width and leaves length alone, so the figure measures 0.48 as
wide as it is long against the 0.57 the published measurements give - 16 to
19.5 mm across at 28 to 34 mm long. Every x measured off the reference is
therefore multiplied by 1.19, the factor that restores that ratio, and the
head is drawn square.
Both corrections are written down rather than quietly applied. A reader
checking this plate against the reference will measure the same 0.48 and is
owed the reason the numbers here differ. It is the same bargain the field
cricket's plate struck - arrangement off the reference, proportions off the
published measurements - and it is struck for the same reason.
## Plate space
y = 0 at the front margin of the clypeus, y = 1000 at the tip of the
pygidium, so the wing cases end at about y = 976 and the last stretch is
abdomen - exactly as on the rose chafer. The middle legs reach past x = 570
and the fore tarsi above y = -100.

note: Legs first, so they pass under the wing cases.
A Christmas beetle is a heavy animal on stout legs, and the tibiae
carry a fringe of stiff spines that Donovan draws one by one. They are
not drawn here: at eighty pixels a spine is a burr on the outline and
six burred limbs read as a smudge. The femora are measured at about
eight per cent of the width across the wing cases rather than the six
CLAUDE.md gives as usual, which is what the reference shows and what
separates a scarab's leg from a ground beetle's.
The fore tibia, toothed on its outer edge for digging. Drawn as a taper
rather than as three separate spurs, for the reason given above the hind
femur: the widening towards the tip is what actually reads.
The pygidium - the last abdominal segment, left uncovered because a
chafer's wing cases stop short of it. Bright green on the living animal
and clothed in pale hair, which is why Donovan gives it a colour of its
own. Drawn behind the elytra so they overlap its front edge, exactly as
the reference shows.
It is also what y = 1000 is measured to. The elytral apex is at about
y = 950 and the last fifty units of this plate are abdomen. Fifty rather
than the twenty-eight of the first pass, which the wing cases covered
entirely - a pygidium that does not clear them is not drawn at all.
One wing case. The suture between the pair is the midline, so the inner
edge of this shape is the axis and the renderer's reflection draws the
other one against it.
The striae. An Anoplognathus is polished rather than deeply grooved, so
what shows is three shallow lines and the raised shoulder - not the eight
sharp furrows a ground beetle gets.
The swell of the wing case, and the correction that took two passes.
It was first drawn as a long panel of bare paper clipped to the elytron -
the gloss every figure of a polished scarab shows. On the page that read
as a pale *marking*, which is the one thing this animal has not got, and
a plate suggesting the rose chafer's flecks on an unmarked beetle keys a
reader to the wrong species. So the highlight became its opposite: five
fine strokes crowding the outer margin, leaving the crown of the case
bare. Shading is what an engraver had, and it cannot be mistaken for a
mark on the animal.
The suture, drawn once on the axis. Reflecting it would lay a second
copy a hair off the first and show as a doubled line down the back.
The pronotum: broad, strongly convex, narrowing forward to about two
thirds of its basal width. It is widest at its own base, where it meets
the wing cases - which is what makes the outline of this animal a single
unbroken oval from the head backwards, and is the first thing to get
right about it.
The head, which on this animal is mostly clypeus: a broad plate, squared
across the front and turned up at the margin, and what a Christmas
beetle pushes soil with.
Donovan draws it cocked a few degrees to the animal's right. It is drawn
square here, because a plate that inherited the tilt would be drawing
that specimen's pose rather than the species.
A lamellate club - three flat plates that open like a fan, and the
character that puts this beetle in the Scarabaeoidea. Drawn as one filled
club with two lines across it, because three separate lamellae at plate
size is three smudges. The record says `lamellate`; this is the drawing
of that word.
